description:
## What happens

Compiling almost any program prints `type/no-matching-clause` warnings that name runtime-library sources rather than the user's program:

```
warning[type/no-matching-clause]: `fn` clauses don't cover every input
  --> runtime:Range.fz:113:3
113 |   fnp reverse([head | tail], acc), do: reverse(tail, [head | acc])
```

The clauses in question are the standard list-accumulator pair:

```
fnp reverse([], acc), do: acc
fnp reverse([head | tail], acc), do: reverse(tail, [head | acc])
```

Those two cover every list. They do not cover every `any`, and the parameter is unannotated, so the declared-domain check is right on its own terms -- `reverse(:atom, [])` really has no clause. But the function is private, its only callers pass lists, and nothing outside the module can reach it with anything else.

The same pattern recurs: `Map.reverse/2`, `Enum.reverse_list/2`, several in `Json`.

## Why it matters

Warnings are errors in this project when they are something we control, and these are ours. They are also load-bearing noise: 24 of the fixture `expected.diagnostics` goldens pin them, so the library's warnings are part of the contract the suite checks, and any comment edit that shifts a line number churns them.

## Two ways out

- Narrow a private function's parameter domain to what its callers actually pass, so an unannotated `fnp` reached only with lists is checked against lists. This is the "correct by construction" answer and removes the warnings rather than hiding them.
- Annotate the parameters in the library. Cheaper, and honest, but it treats the symptom in sixteen files instead of the cause in one.

The first also shrinks the goldens, which is a good independent signal that the noise is gone.
title: The runtime library's own private helpers emit no-matching-clause warnings, pinned in 24 fixture goldens
